plan: SAT R&W batch 71: 9 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000635..000643, weighted toward hard (McClintock WIC, loggerhead magnetic-signature inference, library card-holder two-part quantitative claim, Clovis/Monte Verde cross-text, Semmelweis structure, sociable weaver dangling modifier, Pteropus "however" punctuation, Lake Natron transition, Romer synthesis). Topics checked against every bank and the combined bank. Plus S070-06 (passage adds "with a single exception") and S070-09 (key wording) resubmitted as revision 2 on their previously unbanked passages. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Jumping genes
passages.text: In the 1940s and 1950s, the geneticist Barbara McClintock found evidence that some genes in maize could move from one position on a chromosome to another. For years, many biologists were slow to accept her findings. In the 1970s, however, researchers found such "jumping genes" in bacteria and many other organisms, and McClintock's work was ______: in 1983, she received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

passages.title: The way home
passages.text: Female loggerhead sea turtles often return to nest on or near the beaches where they hatched, sometimes after decades at sea. Each stretch of coastline has a slightly different magnetic signature, determined by the strength and angle of Earth's magnetic field there. Analyzing 19 years of nesting records from Florida, biologists J. Roger Brothers and Kenneth Lohmann found that nesting sites shifted along the coast in step with small, gradual drifts in Earth's magnetic field. This finding suggests that ______

passages.title: Card holders
passages.text:
A student compared the number of library card holders at two branches of a city library.
Eastside: 1,200 in 2019; 1,500 in 2023
Westside: 600 in 2019; 1,200 in 2023
The student claims that Westside's number of card holders grew at a faster rate than Eastside's, even though Eastside still had more card holders in 2023.

passages.title: Who came first?
passages.text:
Text 1
For much of the twentieth century, many archaeologists held that the first people to reach the Americas belonged to the Clovis culture, known from distinctive stone spear points about 13,000 years old. Under this view, no site in the Americas should be much older than the Clovis sites.

Text 2
At Monte Verde in southern Chile, a team led by archaeologist Tom Dillehay excavated wooden structures, stone tools, and food remains that radiocarbon dating placed at about 14,500 years old. In 1997, a group of archaeologists, including several who had doubted the site, visited Monte Verde and agreed that its age was well established.

passages.title: Clean hands
passages.text: In 1847, the physician Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that women giving birth in a Vienna hospital ward staffed by doctors died of fever far more often than those in a ward staffed by midwives. Suspecting that doctors, who often came directly from performing autopsies, were carrying something deadly on their hands, he required them to wash with a chlorine solution, and deaths in their ward dropped sharply. Many physicians rejected his conclusion, and he died in 1865 with his ideas still widely dismissed. Only after scientists such as Louis Pasteur showed that germs cause disease did hand washing become standard medical practice.

passages.title: Apartment builders
passages.text: Sociable weavers, small birds of southern Africa, build enormous communal nests of grass and twigs in trees and on telephone poles, with separate chambers for many pairs of birds. Built and expanded over many years, ______

passages.title: Seeing in the dark
passages.text: Most bats find their way in the dark by echolocation, producing high-pitched calls and listening for the echoes. Large fruit bats of the genus Pteropus, ______ do not echolocate; they rely mainly on their keen eyesight and sense of smell to find fruit and flowers.

passages.title: A harsh nursery
passages.text: Lake Natron in northern Tanzania is so salty and alkaline that its water can burn the skin and eyes of most animals. ______ the lake is the most important breeding site in East Africa for lesser flamingos, which build their nests on islands of salt that form in its shallow waters.

passages.title: Notes on the speed of light
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In the 1670s, Danish astronomer Ole Rømer studied eclipses of Io, one of Jupiter's moons.
- The eclipses happened later than predicted when Earth was farther from Jupiter.
- They happened earlier than predicted when Earth was closer to Jupiter.
- In 1676, Rømer concluded that light takes time to travel across space.
- Before then, many scientists believed that light traveled instantly.

passages.title: A writing system
passages.text: Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith, completed a writing system for the Cherokee language in 1821. Each of the system's symbols, with a single exception, ______ a syllable, which made it unusually quick to learn: within a few years, thousands of Cherokee people could read and write in their own language.

passages.title: Notes on a kitchen discovery
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In the 1880s, scientists growing bacteria often used gelatin as a solid surface.
- Gelatin melts at warm temperatures, and some bacteria break it down.
- Fanny Hesse, who assisted her husband, the physician Walther Hesse, in his laboratory, suggested using agar instead.
- She had used agar to make jellies in her kitchen.
- Agar stays solid at body temperature, and few bacteria can break it down.
- Agar is still widely used to grow bacteria in laboratories.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: researchers found such "jumping genes" in bacteria and many other organisms
candidates.explanation: Later discoveries confirmed what McClintock had found, and she won a Nobel Prize, so her work was "vindicated" (shown to be right).

A.rationale: Her work was confirmed and honored, not replaced by newer work.

C.rationale: The later findings and the Nobel Prize show her work was recognized, not ignored.

D.rationale: Her work came first; the later findings did not anticipate it.

hints: What happened to McClintock's findings after other researchers found jumping genes?
candidates.remember: Use the text after the colon to confirm your prediction.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: loggerhead turtles rely on magnetism alone and ignore every other cue when choosing a nesting site.
choices.B: the beaches where loggerhead turtles nest have moved along the Florida coast over the past 19 years.
choices.C: Earth's magnetic field has drifted in Florida because of changes in where loggerhead turtles nest.
choices.D: the turtles may find their home beaches partly by recognizing the beaches' magnetic signatures.

candidates.evidence: nesting sites shifted along the coast in step with small, gradual drifts
candidates.explanation: If nesting sites move as the magnetic field drifts, the turtles are probably using the magnetic signature to locate their beaches.

A.rationale: The finding is consistent with magnetism as one cue; it does not rule out all others.

B.rationale: The nesting sites shifted; the beaches themselves did not move.

C.rationale: This reverses the relationship: the field drifted, and the nesting followed.

hints: What moved, and what did it move with?

strategy.explanation: Connect the shift to the magnetic signatures described earlier.

candidates.remember: Watch for answers that reverse cause and effect.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's claim?

choices.A: Westside's card holders doubled from 600 to 1,200, while Eastside's rose from 1,200 to 1,500, still above Westside's total.
choices.B: Westside gained 600 card holders between 2019 and 2023, while Eastside gained only 300 card holders over that same period.
choices.C: Eastside had 1,500 card holders in 2023, which was 300 more than the 1,200 card holders that Westside had that year.
choices.D: In 2019, Eastside had twice as many card holders as Westside did, with 1,200 compared with Westside's 600.

candidates.evidence: even though Eastside still had more card holders in 2023
candidates.explanation: The claim has two parts: Westside grew faster (100% versus 25%) and Eastside still had more in 2023 (1,500 versus 1,200). Only this choice supports both.

B.rationale: This compares growth but does not show that Eastside still had more card holders in 2023.

C.rationale: This addresses only the 2023 totals, not the growth rates.

hints: How many parts does the claim have?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against both parts of the claim.

candidates.remember: A two-part claim needs support for both parts.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would Dillehay's team (Text 2) most likely respond to the view described in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the Clovis people were the first to reach South America
choices.B: By claiming that the Clovis spear points are actually much younger than most archaeologists believe
choices.C: By arguing that Monte Verde shows people were in the Americas before the Clovis culture
choices.D: By suggesting that Monte Verde's builders made Clovis-style spear points

candidates.evidence: radiocarbon dating placed at about 14,500 years old
candidates.explanation: A well-dated site about 14,500 years old is older than the roughly 13,000-year-old Clovis sites, which contradicts the Clovis-first view.

A.rationale: Monte Verde is older than Clovis, which contradicts this view.

B.rationale: Text 2 does not discuss the age of Clovis points.

D.rationale: Text 2 does not say Monte Verde had Clovis points.

hints: Is Monte Verde older or younger than Clovis?
candidates.remember: Find the specific point where the texts conflict.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It presents two competing theories about the cause of a disease and then explains why scientists chose one over the other.
choices.B: It describes a discovery and its results, notes the resistance it met, and then explains how it came to be accepted.
choices.C: It describes a medical practice that was widely accepted and then explains why physicians came to abandon it.
choices.D: It compares the working conditions of doctors and midwives and argues that midwives were better trained.

candidates.evidence: Only after scientists such as Louis Pasteur showed
candidates.explanation: The text moves from Semmelweis's observation and successful practice, to its rejection, to its eventual acceptance after germ theory.

A.rationale: Only Semmelweis's conclusion is presented; no competing theory is described.

C.rationale: The practice was first rejected and later accepted, the reverse of this sequence.

D.rationale: The two wards are mentioned only to introduce Semmelweis's observation.

hints: What happens to Semmelweis's idea over time?
candidates.remember: Structure answers must match every part of the text, in order.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the birds sometimes produce nests weighing close to a ton.
choices.B: close to a ton is what some of these nests can weigh.
choices.C: some of these nests can weigh close to a ton.
choices.D: the weight of some of these nests can reach close to a ton.

candidates.evidence: with separate chambers for many pairs of birds
candidates.explanation: "Built and expanded over many years" describes the nests, so "some of these nests" must come right after it.

A.rationale: The opening phrase describes the nests, but "the birds" follows it, so the modifier dangles.

B.rationale: The phrase right after the modifier is "close to a ton," which was not built.

D.rationale: The weight was not built; the modifier must be followed by the nests.

strategy.explanation: Find the noun the opening phrase describes.

candidates.remember: An opening modifier must be followed by the noun it describes.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: they rely mainly on their keen eyesight
candidates.explanation: "However" interrupts the subject and verb of the clause, so it must be set off with commas on both sides.

B.rationale: "However" interrupts the sentence and must be set off by commas on both sides.

C.rationale: A semicolon cannot separate the subject from its verb "do not echolocate."

D.rationale: A colon cannot separate the subject from its verb.

hints: Where does the subject end and the verb begin?
candidates.remember: Set off an interrupting "however" with a pair of commas.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: the most important breeding site in East Africa
candidates.explanation: The lake is harmful to most animals, yet flamingos breed there, so a concessive transition fits.

A.rationale: The second sentence does not restate the first.

B.rationale: The flamingos' breeding is not an example of the lake's harshness.

C.rationale: The second sentence contrasts with the first rather than adding a similar point.

hints: Is the second sentence surprising given the first?
candidates.remember: Use "Even so" for an unexpected result.

candidates.stem: The student wants to present Rømer's conclusion and the evidence that supported it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In the 1670s, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer carefully studied the eclipses of Io, one of the many moons that orbit the planet Jupiter.
choices.B: Because Io's eclipses came later than predicted when Earth was farther from Jupiter, Rømer concluded that light takes time to travel.
choices.C: In 1676, Rømer concluded that light takes time to travel, though many scientists had believed it traveled instantly.
choices.D: Many scientists of the seventeenth century believed that light traveled instantly from one place to another.

candidates.evidence: The eclipses happened later than predicted when Earth was farther from Jupiter
candidates.explanation: Only this choice states both Rømer's conclusion and the observation that supported it.

A.rationale: This describes his observations but gives neither the pattern nor his conclusion.

C.rationale: This gives the conclusion but not the evidence that supported it.

D.rationale: This gives an earlier belief but neither Rømer's conclusion nor his evidence.

hints: Which choice includes both a conclusion and its evidence?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against both parts of the goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must meet every part of the goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The subject is "Each," which is singular, so the singular verb "stands for" is needed.

B.rationale: The subject is the singular "Each," not the plural "symbols."

C.rationale: The plural verb does not agree with the singular "Each."

D.rationale: The plural verb does not agree with the singular "Each."

strategy.explanation: Cross out the prepositional phrase "of the system's symbols."

revision_history.reason: blind solver B: one Cherokee symbol (s) stands for a lone consonant, so "each ... a syllable" overgeneralized

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain why agar was an improvement over gelatin. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Fanny Hesse, who assisted her husband in his laboratory, had used agar to make jellies in her kitchen before suggesting it to him and his colleagues.
choices.B: In the 1880s, scientists who wanted to grow bacteria on a solid surface in their laboratories often used gelatin for that purpose.
choices.C: Agar, which Fanny Hesse suggested in the 1880s, is still widely used today in laboratories around the world to grow bacteria.
choices.D: Unlike gelatin, which melts when warm and is broken down by some bacteria, agar stays solid at body temperature and few bacteria can break it down.

candidates.evidence: Agar stays solid at body temperature
candidates.explanation: Only this choice compares the two materials and gives the properties that make agar better.

A.rationale: This explains where the idea came from, not why agar is better.

B.rationale: This describes gelatin's use but not agar's advantages.

C.rationale: This shows agar's lasting use but does not compare it with gelatin.

hints: Which choice compares agar with gelatin?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must accomplish the stated goal.

revision_history.reason: blind solver A: "resists most bacteria" could imply agar stops bacterial growth
revision_history.change: key now says "few bacteria can break it down"
